\section{Abstract}

Multi-view molecular property prediction --- combining a molecular graph, a SMILES language model and physicochemical descriptors --- is an active area in which new fusion architectures are proposed faster than they are independently checked. We contribute an evaluation protocol strong enough to separate a real gain from a favourable split, and four results obtained by applying it: a large parameter reduction that costs nothing, a free diagnostic for a known uncertainty failure, a proof that a standard calibration step is inert, and a reproducibility requirement that is cheap to adopt.

\textbf{A 71$\times$ smaller fusion block performs identically.} Across eight MoleculeNet datasets and six scaffold splits, a \textbf{16,513-parameter} per-molecule gate matches a \textbf{1,169,793-parameter} cross-attention-plus-bilinear block on every dataset once multiplicity is accounted for. Removing the graph view entirely from the gated model leaves accuracy unmoved (0 improves, 0 degrades; sign test p = 1.00) while training drops from 17 to 1.3 minutes per split, the model shrinks 2.4$\times$, and the graph-library dependency disappears. For deployment this is the operative finding: the cheap configuration is not a compromise.

\textbf{Mean prediction-set size predicts conformal failure, and costs nothing to compute.} A nominal 90\% conformal guarantee covers \textbf{9.7--14.1\% of active compounds} for the three of fifteen models that emit near-singleton sets, and \textbf{71.1--79.8\%} for the other twelve, with nothing in between. The split is visible in mean set size alone --- no labels, no minority statistics --- so a practitioner can tell before deployment which models will fail the class they care about. Class-conditional conformal repairs it at a visible cost in set size. We corroborate the underlying failure, independently reported, and extend it from three model types to fifteen including two published external baselines.

\textbf{Two results that save wasted effort.} Temperature scaling \emph{provably} cannot alter a binary conformal prediction set, so calibrating before conformalizing is a no-op in the binary case; and the adaptive set-valued scores commonly recommended (APS, RAPS) degenerate at two classes. Conformalized quantile regression is the only score we tested whose interval widths carry per-molecule information.

\textbf{Record the accelerator.} A fully seeded pipeline run on a different GPU is a \emph{different model}, moving 18\% of single-split numbers by more than the effect size the field reports differences at. Five-split averaging absorbs it entirely --- the fix is free, and this is the result we think generalises furthest.

The protocol earns these by being harsh, and we report what it costs us as well as what it buys. Our own fusion architecture does not beat a fingerprint-plus-descriptor MLP (4 of 8 datasets, p = 0.55); neither do two published external baselines beat a two-layer graph network. Sweeping the bilinear rank --- a constant chosen once and never examined --- leaves the mechanism's effect unchanged in direction at every rank while its across-dataset significance appears at one rank and vanishes at three, though the ranks are mutually indistinguishable. A multi-split, family-wise-corrected, eight-dataset result can still rest on an arbitrary architectural choice. Applied to our own earlier pipeline, the protocol surfaced six defects that each changed reported numbers, including a missing-label mask that fabricated 24\% of one benchmark's canonical test labels as negatives and a \textbf{0.22 AUC} gap between two procedures both called "scaffold split".

All claims are reproducible from archived per-split predictions, and every headline number in this paper is machine-checked against them.


\section{Introduction}

A molecule can be represented as a graph, as a string, or as a vector of computed physicochemical properties. Each representation is lossy in a different direction, which makes combining them an obvious idea and a recurring one: recent work proposes cross- attention to align views, Kronecker or bilinear products to model second-order interactions between them, and gating to attribute predictions back to views.

These proposals are typically evaluated on a handful of MoleculeNet datasets under a single scaffold split, against baselines drawn from other papers. That evaluation cannot distinguish a real improvement from three other things: a favourable split, a baseline that was not tuned as hard, or a difference smaller than the benchmark's own run-to-run variation. Our starting point is that the last of these is larger than most papers assume.

We therefore built the evaluation first and the architecture second. The protocol (\S3) fixes the leaks and reporting choices we could find, and is deliberately harsh: it uses six splits, pairs every comparison within split, corrects for testing eight datasets at once, and reports the across-dataset test that the per-dataset table cannot substitute for. We then built a five-rung fusion ladder (\S5) so that "fusion helps" could be decomposed into \emph{which mechanism} helps, with a provably additive control at the bottom of the ladder.

An instrument this strict is only worth building if it returns something a weaker one would miss. It does, and the returns are practical rather than architectural: a configuration that is 71$\times$ smaller in its fusion block and 13$\times$ faster to train at identical accuracy, a zero-cost diagnostic for which models will fail their minority class, a proof that one standard calibration step cannot help, and a one-line change to how results are reported that removes an 18\% error rate nobody was accounting for.

\textbf{Contributions.}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{An evaluation protocol} for MoleculeNet property prediction that is leak-free, multi-seed, multiplicity-corrected, and reports both split conventions (\S3), with the minimum detectable effect it implies stated up front: $\pm$0.02 AUC and $\pm$0.10 RMSE.
\item \textbf{A large, free efficiency gain.} A 16,513-parameter gate matches a 1,169,793-parameter fusion block on all eight datasets, and the graph view can be removed outright for a 13$\times$ training speed-up and no measurable accuracy cost (\S5.3, \S5.4).
\item \textbf{Mean prediction-set size as a deployment-time diagnostic} for conformal minority failure, measured across fifteen models and separating them with no overlap --- computable without labels (\S6.2).
\item \textbf{Two results that prevent wasted effort}: temperature scaling provably cannot alter a binary conformal set (\S6.3), and APS/RAPS degenerate at two classes (\S6.4).
\item \textbf{A reproducibility requirement with a free fix}: identical code, seed and splits on a different accelerator produce materially different single-split numbers, and five-split averaging absorbs it entirely (\S7).
\item \textbf{A protocol validation}: applied to our own earlier pipeline, it surfaced six defects that each changed reported numbers (\S4); applied to our own new architecture, it withheld the result we wanted (\S5.6).
\item \textbf{Practical recommendations} distilled from the above for anyone reporting on these benchmarks (\S8), and a dataset-quality audit of duplicate-conflicting labels in three of the eight benchmarks (\S9).
\end{enumerate}

We deliberately do not attempt large-scale self-supervised pretraining, 3D-equivariant architectures, or quantum-chemical descriptor generation. We \emph{use} a pretrained SMILES encoder; we do not pretrain one.

We note for transparency that this paper's framing followed its measurements rather than preceding them: the original plan named the fusion architecture as the primary contribution, the ladder did not support that, and the efficiency and uncertainty results reported here are what the same experiments returned instead. The project record preserves the superseded claim rather than editing it away, which is the strongest evidence we can offer that the protocol was not tuned until it agreed with us.


\section{The evaluation protocol}

\subsection{Datasets}

Eight MoleculeNet datasets: Tox21 (12 tasks), BBBP (1), ClinTox (2), BACE (1) and SIDER (27) for classification; ESOL (logS), Lipophilicity (logD) and FreeSolv (kcal$\cdot$mol⁻¹) for regression.

We dropped HIV from the core protocol. Statistical power across datasets comes from their \emph{number}, not their size: eight datasets put the two-sided signed-rank floor at p = 0.0078, which is sufficient, whereas HIV would have cost roughly 60 GPU-hours for the full protocol without lowering it.

FreeSolv must be loaded from the SAMPL source. The commonly used convenience loader serves an already z-scored target; using it silently reports RMSE in no physical unit.

\subsection{Splits: report both, always}

We report \textbf{both} the canonical DeepChem scaffold split and the mean $\pm$ 95\% CI over five seeded random scaffold splits. These differ by \textbf{up to 0.22 AUC on the same model and the same code} (BBBP, graph baseline: 0.6764 canonical against 0.8959 $\pm$ seeded; the largest gap among the pipeline models, with several others above 0.15). Reporting one is reporting a choice, and which one flatters a given model is not predictable in advance.

The disagreement is not symmetric, and the asymmetry matters more than the spread. Across the \textbf{37} (model, dataset) pairs for which we have both conventions on a classification dataset, the seeded mean is higher than the canonical split on \textbf{33}, with a median difference of \textbf{+0.068 AUC} and \textbf{30} of 37 pairs separated by more than our minimum detectable effect (Figure 4). The canonical DeepChem split is systematically the harder of the two. A paper reporting it and a paper reporting seeded scaffold splits are therefore not comparable even when both say "scaffold split", and the direction of the incomparability is predictable: canonical-split numbers will look worse.

All splits are audited for scaffold leakage (0.0\% in both validation and test) and for train/test index overlap (zero).

\includegraphics[width=0.86\textwidth]{figures/fig4_canonical_vs_seeded.pdf}
\end{center}

\textbf{Figure 4.} Each point is one (model, dataset) pair on a classification benchmark. Points above the diagonal are those the canonical split scores lower than the mean of five seeded scaffold splits. Generated by \code{python -m scripts.make\_figures}.

\subsection{Fitting discipline}

\code{train} fits models. A \code{fit}/\code{cal} sub-split carved from train --- or out-of-fold predictions over train --- fits everything downstream: the meta-learner, the ensemble weights, the calibrators, the decision thresholds. \code{valid} is used for early stopping and hyper-parameter choice only. \code{test} is touched once.

\subsection{Comparisons: three levels, reported together}

Splits differ in difficulty far more than models differ from each other, so every comparison is \textbf{paired within split}. We then report three things, because they answer different questions and do not always agree:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Per-dataset}: is the mean paired difference larger than its own 95\% interval?
\item \textbf{Per-dataset, Holm--Bonferroni corrected} across the eight datasets. Eight tests at $\alpha$ = 0.05 produce at least one false positive 34\% of the time, and several conclusions in this area rest on exactly one decisive dataset out of eight.
\item \textbf{Across datasets}: one test over eight paired observations, reported as a sign test, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test on Cohen's \emph{dz}, and a Wilcoxon on raw differences. The last of these ranks an AUC point against a logS point, which is not a commensurable comparison; we report it because it is what is usually done, and we report the other two because it is not sufficient.
\end{enumerate}

With n = 5 splits the per-dataset Wilcoxon cannot go below p = 0.0625, so a clean 5--0 sweep is not significance; we use the paired difference's own interval instead and say so.

\subsection{Minimum detectable effect}

Measured from the baseline's across-seed intervals: \textbf{$\pm$0.02 AUC, $\pm$0.10 RMSE}. A difference smaller than this is inside the benchmark's own noise and we do not call it a result, even when it is statistically clear.

\subsection{One hyper-parameter setting}

Every model is trained under a single fixed hyper-parameter setting, recorded in \code{configs/shared.yaml} and asserted against the trainers' actual defaults by a check that fails when they drift. This makes the comparisons fair and leaves absolute numbers untuned; we consider that the right trade and state it as a limitation (\S10). No architecture in this paper has been tuned, including ours.


\section{Protocol validation: six defects it surfaces}

We re-ran our own earlier multi-model pipeline under the protocol above. Six defects each changed reported numbers.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A dropped missing-label mask.} Tox21 is sparsely measured. The mask marking unmeasured (compound, assay) pairs was not propagated, so unmeasured entries were trained and scored as negatives --- \textbf{23.9\% of the canonical test labels}.
\item \textbf{Regression metrics in z-scored units}, so errors were unitless rather than in logS or kcal$\cdot$mol⁻¹.
\item \textbf{Model selection on test.}
\item \textbf{Four fitted stages on one validation split} --- meta-learner, ensemble weights, calibrators, thresholds --- with the improvement then reported on that same split.
\item \textbf{A "frozen" encoder running with dropout active}, and computed bond features discarded before message passing.
\item \textbf{No seeding} outside one component, making every reported neural number a single unreproducible draw.
\end{enumerate}

Re-running under the fixed protocol moves the numbers substantially and in both directions; Table 1 reports the corrected baseline. Two representative rows: Tox21 goes from 0.7514 AUC on the canonical split to 0.8223 $\pm$ 0.0239 across seeded splits, and ESOL from 1.1463 to 0.9778 $\pm$ 0.0984 logS.

We also found and fixed two defects in \textbf{our own} evaluation before trusting it: a significance rule that tested the mean difference against the \emph{reference model's} spread rather than the paired difference's own (producing contradictory verdicts --- a 0--5 loss at p = 0.018 called "inside noise" while a weaker p = 0.027 was called a degradation), and a head-width confound in which the prediction head was sized from each encoder's output width, so a sequence view trained a 2.36M-parameter head against a 147k-parameter adapter. Every Phase 1 result was re-measured after the second fix.


\section{Case study: the multi-view fusion ladder}

\subsection{Views}

Five single-view baselines, each projected to a common 256-dimensional width before an identically sized head, so that comparisons differ in representation and nothing else: the 2-layer GIN from our earlier pipeline (\code{gin\_ref}); an edge-aware GINE encoder; a frozen SMILES transformer (CLS $\oplus$ mean pooling); the same transformer with LoRA adapters; and an ECFP $\oplus$ 217 RDKit 2-D descriptor MLP.

\textbf{No single view replaces the baseline graph encoder.} After correction, \code{gine} improves on 0 of 8 datasets at five times the parameters; the descriptor MLP on 0 of 8; the sequence views on 1 while degrading on 1.

Two findings survive:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{LoRA helps only where the frozen encoder was weak.} Against a \emph{matched frozen control} it improves on ESOL (p = 0.0071 after correction) and nowhere else, and both of its uncorrected wins are regression datasets. Without that control, its 0.9888 AUC on ClinTox would have read as evidence for fine-tuning when it is attributable to pooling and pretraining. This is the only per-dataset finding anywhere in this work that survives family-wise correction.
\item \textbf{Leading by mean is not winning.} The descriptor view leads 6 of 8 datasets by mean and is decisive on none. Three of those leads are datasets where the descriptors encode the target's own physics: the classical ESOL solubility equation is a linear function of descriptors in this set, and topological polar surface area alone correlates with hydration free energy at r = −0.736 (r² = 0.542) on FreeSolv.
\end{itemize}

The views are strongly complementary, which is the premise fusion needs: the best-to-worst spread reaches 0.148 AUC on ClinTox, and the ordering \emph{reverses} between datasets --- the descriptor view is best on FreeSolv and worst on ClinTox, the sequence views the opposite.

\subsection{The ladder}

Five fusion strategies behind one interface, each removing one mechanism:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
rung & mechanism & fusion parameters (3 views, d=256) \\
\midrule
\code{concat} & none --- stack and project & 0 \\
\code{gated} & per-molecule softmax over views & \textbf{16,513} \\
\code{xattn} & views as tokens, cross-attention & 1,054,208 \\
\code{bilinear} & low-rank pairwise second-order term & 99,072 \\
\code{proposed} & xattn $\rightarrow$ bilinear $\rightarrow$ gate & \textbf{1,169,793} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{Every rung was verified to compute the kind of function it claims} before any of its results were interpreted. For a function of three views, the second-order interaction between two of them is the mixed difference \emph{D} = \emph{f}(a,b,c) − \emph{f}(a′,b,c) − \emph{f}(a,b′,c) + \emph{f}(a′,b′,c). If \emph{f} is additive in its views this cancels exactly, whatever the per-view functions are; a non-zero \emph{D} is proof the module mixes views multiplicatively rather than merely stacking them.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lllll}
\toprule
rung & max \textbackslash\{\} & \emph{D}\textbackslash\{\} &  &  \\
\midrule
\code{concat} & 2.4 $\times$ 10⁻⁷ & additive to float32 cancellation &  &  \\
\code{gated} & 4.5 $\times$ 10⁻¹ & interacting &  &  \\
\code{xattn} & 1.1 $\times$ 10⁰ & interacting &  &  \\
\code{bilinear} & 1.1 $\times$ 10¹ & interacting &  &  \\
\code{proposed} & 1.3 $\times$ 10¹ & interacting &  &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Seven orders of magnitude separate the additive control from the cheapest interacting rung, so \code{concat} is a genuine additive floor and the ladder's logic holds. \textbf{The negative results below are not a broken implementation.} Reproduce with \code{python -m scripts.check\_mechanisms}, which exits non-zero if any rung stops behaving as its name claims.

Four readings, in decreasing order of confidence:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{The fusion model beats the baseline graph encoder decisively and on every dataset.} This is a real result and it is the one a conventional paper would report alone. It is also narrower than it looks, and the next table is why.
\item \textbf{It does not beat the strongest single view.} A descriptor MLP over fingerprints and computed properties is statistically indistinguishable from a 1.17M-parameter fusion block over three representations.
\item \textbf{Learned combination beats naive concatenation} --- but this is unit-dependent (significant on both Wilcoxon variants, not on the unit-free sign test) and must be reported with all three numbers.
\item \textbf{The expensive mechanisms buy nothing over a cheap gate} --- which we state as the efficiency result it is. \code{proposed} over \code{gated} is 1 of 8 uncorrected (BACE, p = 0.017), \textbf{0 of 8 after correction} (p $\rightarrow$ 0.135), and shows no across-dataset difference. Cross-attention (1.05M parameters) and the bilinear block (99k) together buy one dataset that does not survive multiplicity. Read the other way round: \textbf{the 16,513-parameter gate delivers the 1,169,793-parameter block's accuracy at 1/71st of the fusion capacity}, and a practitioner who adopts it loses nothing this protocol can detect.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Against the full earlier pipeline, not just its graph encoder.} \code{gin\_ref} is a deliberately simple ablation reference --- the 2-layer GIN --- and beating it is not the same as beating the system it sat inside. The pipeline's five models cover five of our eight datasets, so the comparison is run there (n = 5, where the sign test cannot go below p = 0.0625):

\textbf{End-to-end adaptation buys nothing.} Training LoRA adapters inside the fusion model rather than reading cached frozen embeddings gives 0 improvements and 0 degradations across 8 datasets, with 7 of 8 means favouring the cached version, for roughly 11 GPU-hours. The end-to-end ladder is nonetheless useful as an independent replication of the mechanism attribution in \S5.6, having been trained months later on different hardware.

\subsection{Gate weights measure routing, not necessity}

The gate assigns the graph view \textbf{0.4--1.1\%} of the weight on every dataset, and its preferred view matches the measured best single view on \textbf{7 of 8} --- so the weights are not noise.

We then removed the graph view and retrained. Accuracy did not move (0 improves, 0 degrades after correction; no across-dataset difference: sign test p = 1.00, Wilcoxon on \emph{dz} p = 0.64) while cost collapsed:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
 & full & no graph \\
\midrule
time per split & 17 min & \textbf{1.3 min} \\
parameters (FreeSolv) & 2,050,694 & \textbf{848,514} \\
graph library dependency & required & \textbf{none} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

But removing a view holding 0.4\% of the weight \textbf{rewrote the other two weights}: the descriptor weight moved +0.487 on BACE, +0.389 on SIDER and +0.362 on BBBP, whose preferred view flipped outright from sequence to descriptor --- while accuracy stayed flat.

\textbf{Gate weights are a readout of how one trained model routed information, not a measure of how much each view matters.} Both facts are needed: the agreement check says the weights are not noise, the ablation says they are not necessity. Interpretability claims built on attention or gate weights should be accompanied by the corresponding removal experiment.

\subsection{An external baseline}

Every comparison so far is internal: our models against each other and against the pipeline we started from. That is the weakest kind of evidence, because it cannot rule out that the whole family is poor. We therefore ran \textbf{AttentiveFP}, a widely used attention-based graph architecture, through the \emph{identical} protocol --- same splits, same 256-d projection, same head, same fixed hyper-parameters, same accelerator. What remains distinctively AttentiveFP is its message passing and its attention-based graph readout; what is held constant is everything else. A baseline trained under its own author's recipe and compared against ours would confound the architecture with the training protocol, which is the failure this paper exists to document.

comparison & favoured & sign & \emph{dz} & raw & after Holm \\
\midrule

AttentiveFP vs \code{gin\_ref} (baseline)* & 6/8 & 0.2891 & 0.1953 & 0.1094 & 0 / 0 \\
\textbf{Chemprop vs \code{gin\_ref}} & 4/8 & 1.0000 & 0.9453 & 0.8438 & 0 / 0 \\
Chemprop vs AttentiveFP & 4/8 & 1.0000 & 1.0000 & 1.0000 & 0 / 0 \\
AttentiveFP vs \code{desc} & 2/8 & 0.2891 & 0.1484 & 0.3125 & 0 / 0 \\
\textbf{Chemprop vs \code{desc}} & 2/8 & 0.2891 & 0.1094 & 0.3828 & 0 / \textbf{1} \\
\textbf{\code{proposed} vs AttentiveFP} & \textbf{7/8} & 0.0703 & 0.0547 & 0.0547 & 0 / 0 \\
\textbf{\code{proposed} vs Chemprop} & \textbf{6/8} & 0.2891 & 0.1094 & 0.1953 & \textbf{2} / 0 \\

\end{center}

\textbackslash\{\}* Against the accelerator-matched instance of every baseline, per \S7: AttentiveFP ran on the same hardware as the models it is compared with here, so none of these is a cross-hardware comparison.

Three readings.

\textbf{AttentiveFP beats our edge-aware graph encoder} (unit-dependent: significant on both Wilcoxon variants, not on the sign test) at roughly twice the parameters --- 1,986,304 against 1,070,852. That is the expected direction, and it is reassuring that the protocol detects it: the published architecture is better than the one we built to represent it.

\textbf{Neither external baseline beats the 2-layer GIN baseline.} AttentiveFP is favoured on 6 of 8 and Chemprop on 4 of 8, with no across-dataset difference on any statistic and nothing surviving correction --- AttentiveFP at nearly ten times the baseline encoder's parameters (1,986,304 against 207,360). The two published methods are also indistinguishable from \emph{each other} (4/8, p = 1.00 on all three statistics).

\textbf{Neither beats a fingerprint-plus-descriptor MLP either.} \code{desc} is favoured over each of them on 6 of 8, and decisively beats Chemprop on one dataset after correction. A pair of well-regarded graph architectures, trained on the same splits with the same budget, do not separate from a multilayer perceptron over computed chemistry.

\textbf{Our fusion model is favoured over both and reaches significance against neither across datasets} --- 7 of 8 over AttentiveFP (0.055--0.070), 6 of 8 over Chemprop (0.11--0.29), though 2 datasets survive correction in the Chemprop comparison. The plan's criterion was to be \emph{competitive with or beating} a strong external baseline on most datasets. \textbf{Competitive is met on both; beating is not established on either}, and with n = 8 the sign test cannot reach 0.05 from a 7--1 split however large the effect.

One inconsistency deserves stating rather than hiding: AttentiveFP beats \code{gine}, AttentiveFP ties \code{gin\_ref}, and \code{gine} ties \code{gin\_ref}. Those three cannot all be strictly true of an underlying ordering. With eight paired observations the tests are underpowered enough that intransitive verdicts are expected, and reading any single one of them as an ordering is exactly the over-reading this protocol is built to prevent.

The wider point is the one the whole ladder makes. Two published graph architectures --- one attention-based, one a directed message-passing network --- a bond-aware graph encoder, a pretrained language model and a three-view fusion block are, on these eight benchmarks under a controlled protocol, all statistically indistinguishable from a two-layer graph network and from a multilayer perceptron over fingerprints and computed descriptors.

\subsection{Which mechanism does the work?}

The ladder was built so that "fusion helps" could be decomposed. With the end-to-end rungs now complete, it can be. The question is whether \code{proposed}'s advantage comes from cross-attention (the mechanism one source proposes) or from the explicit second-order bilinear term (the mechanism the other proposes).

Reported in three settings: the committed cached ladder (frozen embeddings, CPU), the same cached ladder regenerated on a T4, and the end-to-end ladder with LoRA adapters trained. The first two differ only in hardware, which \S7 shows is noise in the five-split mean; the third is a genuinely different training regime. Across-dataset Wilcoxon on \emph{dz}:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
comparison & cached, CPU & cached, T4 & end-to-end, T4 \\
\midrule
\code{bilinear} vs \code{concat} & 7/8, \textbf{p = 0.039} & 8/8, \textbf{p = 0.008} & 6/8, p = 0.078 \\
\code{xattn} vs \code{concat} & 5/8, p = 0.641 & 5/8, p = 0.547 & 4/8, p = 0.383 \\
\code{proposed} vs \code{bilinear} & 5/8, p = 0.313 & 3/8, p = 0.547 & 6/8, p = 0.148 \\
\textbf{\code{proposed} vs \code{xattn}} & 6/8, p = 0.078 & 7/8, p = 0.109 & 7/8, \textbf{p = 0.016} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The pattern is the same in all three and points one way:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{The bilinear term is doing the work.} It is the only single mechanism that separates from plain concatenation, and it is favoured on 6 to 8 of 8 datasets in every setting.
\item \textbf{Cross-attention is not.} It is indistinguishable from concatenation in all three (p = 0.38 to 0.64), and \code{proposed} is consistently better than \code{xattn} alone --- meaning what \code{proposed} adds over cross-attention is precisely the bilinear block.
\item \textbf{\code{proposed} is indistinguishable from \code{bilinear} alone} in all three. The 1,054,208 cross-attention parameters buy nothing on top of the 99,072-parameter bilinear block.
\end{itemize}

So of the two mechanisms the literature proposes, one survives this evaluation in weakened form and the other does not survive at all.

\subsubsection{The rank sweep, and what it does to the claim above}

The bilinear block's rank \emph{r} sets the size of the second-order interaction: two \emph{d} $\times$ \emph{r} projections per view pair in place of a full \emph{d} $\times$ \emph{d} form. Every result above used r = 64, chosen once. Having just identified this block as the mechanism that works, the obvious question is whether that choice made it work. We trained r ∈ \{16, 32, 128\} on the same splits, on the same hardware as the cached-T4 column, changing nothing else.

\textbf{No rank is distinguishable from any other.} Against r = 64, each of r = 16, 32 and 128 gives 0 improves, 0 degrades, 8 indistinguishable. The extremes --- a 24,768-parameter interaction against a 198,144-parameter one, eight times apart --- differ at p = 0.844. The block is inert to its own capacity across the entire span.

But against the ladder floor, the comparison the claim rests on, the ranks do not agree:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llllll}
\toprule
rank & fusion parameters & favoured vs \code{concat} & sign & \emph{dz} & raw \\
\midrule
16 & 24,768 & 6/8 & 0.289 & 0.055 & 0.195 \\
32 & 49,536 & 6/8 & 0.289 & 0.109 & 0.109 \\
\textbf{64} & \textbf{99,072} & \textbf{8/8} & \textbf{0.008} & \textbf{0.008} & \textbf{0.008} \\
128 & 198,144 & 6/8 & 0.289 & 0.078 & 0.148 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Only r = 64 reaches significance, and p = 0.008 is the \emph{floor} for n = 8 --- the smallest value the sign test can return, reachable only by a clean sweep. The per-dataset means say why (mean paired difference against \code{concat}, positive favouring bilinear):

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lllll}
\toprule
dataset & r = 16 & r = 32 & r = 64 & r = 128 \\
\midrule
Tox21 & +0.0121 & +0.0125 & +0.0142 & +0.0154 \\
ClinTox & +0.0171 & +0.0082 & +0.0162 & +0.0100 \\
\textbf{SIDER} & \textbf{+0.0535} & \textbf{+0.0626} & \textbf{+0.0730} & \textbf{+0.0629} \\
Lipophilicity & +0.0045 & +0.0016 & +0.0007 & +0.0017 \\
FreeSolv & +0.0629 & +0.0774 & +0.0722 & +0.0363 \\
BBBP & +0.0045 & −0.0018 & +0.0015 & −0.0007 \\
BACE & −0.0047 & +0.0031 & +0.0065 & +0.0065 \\
ESOL & −0.0134 & −0.0048 & +0.0129 & −0.0276 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Five datasets favour the bilinear term at every rank. Three change sign --- BBBP, BACE, ESOL --- and every one of those changes is far below our own minimum detectable effect (\S3.5): BBBP moves within $\pm$0.005 AUC, BACE within $\pm$0.007 AUC, ESOL within $\pm$0.03 RMSE, against thresholds of $\pm$0.02 and $\pm$0.10. Only SIDER exceeds the MDE, and it does so at every rank.

The direction therefore holds across six separately trained bilinear models --- the three settings above plus these three ranks --- favoured on 6 to 8 of 8 every time and never once reversed. What moves between p = 0.008 and p = 0.109 is which way three datasets sitting at effectively zero happen to land.

\subsubsection{This is our own result failing our own standard}

\code{bilinear}(r = 64) beats \code{concat} significantly. \code{bilinear}(r = 16) does not. And \code{bilinear}(r = 64) versus \code{bilinear}(r = 16) is \emph{also} not significant, at p = 0.641. That is exactly the error Gelman and Stern name: the difference between "significant" and "not significant" is not itself significant.

We report it because it is the same failure this paper spends its length documenting, one level up. \S3.2 shows a single scaffold split producing a 0.22 AUC swing; \S7 shows a seeded pipeline producing a different model on different hardware. Those are arguments that single-run results do not survive scrutiny. This is a \emph{multi-split, Holm-corrected, eight-dataset} result whose significance still turns on an architectural constant chosen once and never examined --- and we would not have known had we not run the ablation. A reader is entitled to ask how many published fusion results rest on a comparably arbitrary choice that was never swept. We cannot answer that, and neither could we have answered it about our own until we looked.

The honest statement of \S5.6 is therefore: the bilinear term is the mechanism that separates from concatenation, the effect is real, small, and concentrated in one dataset, and its across-dataset p-value is not stable to a hyper-parameter that does not otherwise matter.

\textbf{But neither clears the cheap baseline.} Against the 16,513-parameter gate in the end-to-end setting, \code{xattn} is favoured on 3 of 8 and \code{bilinear} on 3 of 8, with nothing surviving correction in either case. The second-order term beats naive concatenation and still does not beat a per-molecule volume knob. That is the finding in one line: \textbf{the mechanism that works is not the expensive one, and the mechanism that is expensive does not work.}


\section{Calibration and conformal uncertainty}

\subsection{Post-hoc calibration mostly does not transfer}

Across 65 (model, dataset) pairs and five seeded splits, fitting a temperature or Platt map and evaluating test ECE: calibration \textbf{decisively helps on 20, hurts on 1, and is inside its own interval on 44}. Where it helps it helps the worst-calibrated models and never rescues one that was already well calibrated. A map fitted on one partition largely does not transfer to a scaffold-shifted test set by more than that partition's own noise --- and on one pair (Chemprop on SIDER, 0.106 to 0.113) it transfers in the wrong direction.

\subsection{The guarantee is met by covering the wrong molecules}

Split conformal was validated to nominal on synthetic data (90.1 / 90.1 / 90.3\% at a 90\% target) before use, so gaps on real data are findings rather than bugs.

On Tox21 at a nominal 90\%, marginal coverage is met by every model --- and the minority class is not covered:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
model & overall & \textbf{actives} & mean set size \\
\midrule
SMILES transformer & 91.0\% & \textbf{9.7\%} & 0.99 \\
Random forest & 90.7\% & \textbf{9.8\%} & 0.98 \\
\textbf{Chemprop} & 90.6\% & \textbf{14.1\%} & 0.97 \\
\code{fuse\_gated\_nograph} & 89.9\% & 71.1\% & 1.16 \\
\code{fuse\_concat} & 89.8\% & 71.3\% & 1.19 \\
\code{fuse\_gated} & 90.3\% & 72.4\% & 1.17 \\
\code{fuse\_proposed} & 89.4\% & 72.7\% & 1.20 \\
\code{gin\_ref} & 89.8\% & 76.8\% & 1.26 \\
\code{desc} & 90.0\% & 77.9\% & 1.21 \\
AttentiveFP & 90.3\% & 79.8\% & 1.23 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The catastrophic failure is \textbf{not an outlier but a mechanism, and mean set size predicts it.} Across \textbf{15 models} on Tox21 the column splits cleanly in two, with nothing in between:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
group & models & actives covered \\
\midrule
mean set size $\leq$ 1.05 & 3 (random forest, SMILES transformer, \textbf{Chemprop}) & \textbf{9.7 -- 14.1\%} \\
mean set size > 1.05 & 12 (everything else) & 71.1 -- 79.8\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

A \textbf{57-point gap} separates the two groups. On data that is 6--9\% positive, a marginal 90\% guarantee can be satisfied by emitting confident singletons of the majority class, and set size is exactly the diagnostic for whether a model is doing that. It costs nothing to compute and it tells you \emph{which} models will fail before you look at per-class coverage.

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.86\textwidth]{figures/fig1_setsize_vs_minority_coverage.pdf}
\end{center}

\textbf{Figure 1.} Fifteen models on Tox21 under marginal split conformal at a nominal 90\%. The horizontal axis needs no labels, no minority statistics and no held-out actives to compute; the vertical axis needs all three. The shaded band is empty --- no model in this study sits between the two groups. Generated by \code{python -m scripts.make\_figures}.

The practical consequence is that the diagnostic is available \emph{before} deployment. Minority coverage requires a labelled evaluation set with enough actives to estimate it; mean set size requires only the model's own outputs on unlabelled molecules. A team choosing between candidate models for a screening campaign can rank them on this axis without running the experiment that would tell them the answer directly.

That a well-regarded published method (Chemprop) sits in the failing group alongside a random forest is the part worth emphasising: this is not a property of weak models.

Within the larger group, every architecture --- including every rung of the fusion ladder and both external baselines --- under-covers actives by 10--19 points, and the spread between the best and worst (71.1\% to 79.8\%) is \textbf{smaller than any of their gaps to nominal}. The under-coverage there is a property of the data and the method, not of the model.

\textbf{Class-conditional (Mondrian) conformal repairs it}, fitting a separate quantile per class: actives rise to 87--91\% for every model, with the price openly visible in mean set size (0.98 $\rightarrow$ 1.52 for the random forest; \textasciitilde{}1.2 $\rightarrow$ \textasciitilde{}1.4 for the fusion ladder).

\textbf{This result is not ours first.} Tursunbadalov \& Tursunbadalov (arXiv:2607.06605, July 2026) report the same failure and the same fix, independently and four months before this draft: on four datasets marginal conformal meets its global 90\% target while minority coverage falls to 64.8\% on BBBP, 38.9\% on a Tox21 endpoint and 4.2\% on ClinTox, it reproduces across a random forest, a graph network and a frozen chemical language model, and class-conditional conformal closes it for a modest increase in set size. Their conservation identity --- the minority's shortfall equals the majority's surplus amplified by the imbalance ratio --- is a cleaner explanation of the magnitude than anything we offer.

We report our measurement as \textbf{independent corroboration on a wider model set}, not as a discovery. What it adds is breadth and one mechanism: fifteen models including every rung of a fusion ladder and two published external baselines, where the spread across the twelve architectures that cover the minority class at all (71.1\% to 79.8\%) is smaller than any of their gaps to nominal, and where the three that fail are exactly the three whose mean set size is $\approx$ 1.0 --- on 6--9\% positive data, a marginal guarantee can be met with confident singletons of the majority class. That one of the three is Chemprop, a method a practitioner would actually reach for, is what makes this a property of the setting rather than of weak models. The set-size diagnostic is complementary to their coverage-gap diagnostic, costs nothing to compute, and predicts \emph{which} models will fail.

The rest of \S6 does not overlap with their work: \S6.3's invariance proof, \S6.4's analysis of APS/RAPS at two classes, \S6.5's regression scores and \S6.6's distance stratification are, as far as we can determine, not covered there.

\subsection{Temperature scaling provably cannot change a binary conformal set}

The conformal score is \code{1 − p} for an active and \code{p} for an inactive, and the temperature map \code{g} is symmetric about 0.5: \code{max |g(1−p) − (1 − g(p))| $\approx$ 2 $\times$ 10⁻¹⁶} across the probability range. Both classes therefore pass through the \emph{same} strictly increasing map, the calibration quantile moves with them, and every \code{score $\leq$ q} comparison is preserved. Split conformal is invariant to monotone transformations of its score, so nothing can change. We verified the sets bit-identical while the underlying probabilities moved by up to 0.02.

Platt scaling has an intercept, is not symmetric, and does change things --- recovering actives to 85.7\% on Tox21, but as a side effect of fitting with balanced class weights rather than by any guarantee, and landing short of the nominal 90\%.

This matters because "calibrate, then conformalize" is a natural pipeline to build, and for binary tasks with this score it is provably wasted effort.

\subsection{Adaptive set scores degenerate at two classes}

APS and RAPS are the standard recommendations for set-valued classification. At two classes they are unusable:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
score & Tox21 coverage & mean set size (max 2) \\
\midrule
LAC (\code{1 − p(true class)}) & 90.7\% & \textbf{0.98} \\
APS & 99.9\% & 1.98 \\
RAPS & 96.5\% & 1.27 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

APS answers "could be either" for essentially every molecule. The reason is structural: with two classes the lower-ranked class always scores exactly 1.0, so the calibration scores collapse onto a spike, and any model emitting saturated probabilities (a random forest with unanimous votes does so for 15\% of Tox21 molecules) places \emph{top-class} scores on that same spike. When the quantile lands there, the lower-ranked class is admitted for every molecule.

RAPS is \textbf{not} identical to APS here, which is the natural assumption --- its rank penalty adds a constant to the lower-ranked class and so appears to be a monotone map on the score, to which conformal is invariant. It is not: the penalty is a function of the \emph{class}, not the score. What it does is break the tie at the spike, and that alone changes mean set size from 2.000 to 1.000.

\subsection{Interval width, and what carries information}

For regression, the choice of score determines whether the interval says anything:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
score & ESOL coverage & mean width & width s.d. \\
\midrule
absolute residual (constant width) & 85.1\% & 2.215 & \textbf{0.000} \\
normalised by base-model disagreement & 91.9\% & \textbf{7.071} & 3.979 \\
\textbf{conformalized quantile regression} & 87.7\% & \textbf{2.509} & \textbf{0.821} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The constant-width score is correct and useless: every molecule receives the same interval, so it cannot indicate which predictions to distrust. Normalising by an ensemble-disagreement proxy makes width vary but buys that adaptivity by inflating every interval --- three times the width. CQR, fitting explicit conditional quantiles with pinball loss, is the only score we tested that varies width meaningfully at a usable mean width. It under-covers by 2--4 points, which is the same exchangeability failure documented next.

\subsection{Coverage decays with distance from the training set}

Binning Tox21 test molecules by Tanimoto similarity to their nearest training neighbour, averaged over the same fifteen models and six splits as \S6.2:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
similarity & mean n & overall & \textbf{actives} \\
\midrule
0.0--0.3 (most novel) & 74 & 88.4\% & \textbf{49.0\%} \\
0.3--0.4 & 161 & 88.6\% & 58.4\% \\
0.4--0.5 & 179 & 89.7\% & 61.8\% \\
0.5--0.7 & 255 & 90.1\% & 69.4\% \\
0.7--1.0 (close analogues) & 114 & 92.5\% & 65.5\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Overall coverage falls monotonically from 92.5\% to 88.4\% --- a 4-point drift that a marginal guarantee can absorb almost unnoticed. Active coverage falls from 69.4\% to \textbf{49.0\%}, so on the molecules a scaffold split exists to test, a nominal 90\% guarantee covers barely half the compounds a screen is run to find. (The actives column is \emph{not} monotone at the top: the most-similar band sits at 65.5\% on \textasciitilde{}114 molecules with a low positive rate, which we read as sampling noise rather than a reversal, and report rather than smooth.)

This is the exchangeability assumption failing, measured rather than argued, and it is the mechanism behind \S6.2: the models that emit near-singleton sets are the ones that resolve this tension by abandoning the minority class everywhere rather than only at the far end.

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.86\textwidth]{figures/fig2_coverage_by_distance.pdf}
\end{center}

\textbf{Figure 2.} The two lines are the same guarantee, read two ways. The blue line is what a marginal conformal report shows; the red line is what a screening campaign experiences. Generated by \code{python -m scripts.make\_figures}.

\subsection{Activity cliffs}

A test molecule is \emph{on a cliff} if another molecule in the dataset is within ECFP Tanimoto 0.9 and carries the opposite label. Comparing cliff to non-cliff molecules within the same test set and the same model:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lllll}
\toprule
dataset & model & cliff & non-cliff & penalty \\
\midrule
BACE (13 / 139) & \code{desc} & 0.5025 & 0.8447 & +0.3421 \\
BACE & \code{fuse\_gated} & 0.5338 & 0.8245 & +0.2906 \\
Tox21 (34 / 749) & \code{desc} & 0.7148 & 0.8327 & +0.1179 \\
Tox21 & \code{fuse\_gated} & 0.6883 & 0.8323 & +0.1439 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

On BACE every model is \textbf{at chance} on cliff molecules while scoring 0.82--0.84 on the rest. Fusion helps on BACE and ClinTox and hurts slightly on Tox21. Cliff sets are 10--34 molecules, so this is directional rather than decisive, and the ordering is stable at a 0.85 threshold.


\section{Seeded is not reproducible across hardware}

We regenerated five models under identical code, identical seeds and identical split indices, on a different accelerator. Of 240 test metrics present in both runs, \textbf{only 4 were identical}; the median absolute difference was 0.033 and the largest was 0.4514 RMSE.

The cause is not a seeding defect. Weight initialisation occurs on CPU before transfer and matches exactly; dropout masks are drawn \emph{on device}, so a CPU run and a CUDA run draw from different generators. Different masks, different optimisation trajectory, different model.

Scaled by this work's own minimum detectable effect:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
reporting unit & median & max & fraction exceeding MDE \\
\midrule
single canonical split & 0.34 $\times$ MDE & \textbf{2.16 $\times$ MDE} & \textbf{7 of 40 (18\%)} \\
mean over 5 seeded splits & 0.26 $\times$ MDE & 1.00 $\times$ MDE & 1 of 40 (2\%) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Under the paired test we report, the device effect is \textbf{not detectable at all}: 0 improves, 0 degrades and 8 indistinguishable on all five models, with no across-dataset difference.

The per-split differences are noise, not bias --- they are large, and they average out. We consider this the strongest available justification for multi-seed reporting: the protocol was built to absorb split-to-split variance and it absorbs hardware variance too, while the single-split number it replaces does not. \textbf{Nearly one in five canonical-split numbers moves by more than the effect size the field reports differences at, from nothing but a change of GPU.}

A practical consequence: benchmark tables should record the accelerator, and cross-hardware comparisons of single-split numbers should be treated as uncontrolled.


\section{Practical recommendations}

Everything below follows from a measurement in this paper, and each is cheap enough to adopt immediately.

\textbf{For anyone training these models.}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Try the cheap configuration first, and make it prove it is worse.} A 16,513-parameter gate matched a 1,169,793-parameter fusion block on all eight datasets (\S5.3), and dropping the graph view left accuracy unmoved while cutting training from 17 to 1.3 minutes per split and removing the graph-library dependency entirely (\S5.4). Neither saving was available to us until we built the comparison that could detect its absence.
\item \textbf{Include a descriptor baseline.} An ECFP-plus-descriptor MLP was favoured over our fusion model on 4 of 8 datasets (p = 0.55) and over a published external baseline on one dataset after correction (\S5.5). It trains in minutes. A multi-view result that is not compared against it is not yet a result.
\item \textbf{Fix one hyper-parameter setting across every arm.} Tuning one side of a comparison against fixed-setting baselines measures search budget, not architecture. We state the setting in a machine-checked configuration file (\S3.6).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{For anyone reporting on these benchmarks.}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Report both split conventions, or say which one you used.} Two procedures both called "scaffold split" differ by up to 0.22 AUC on the same model and the same code (\S3.2).
\item \textbf{Average over several splits, and record the accelerator.} Identical code, seed and splits on a different GPU moved 18\% of single-split numbers by more than the effect size the field reports differences at; the five-split mean absorbed it entirely (\S7). Recording the device costs one column.
\item \textbf{State a minimum detectable effect before reading the results.} Ours is $\pm$0.02 AUC and $\pm$0.10 RMSE (\S3.5). Differences below it should not be described as improvements.
\item \textbf{Correct for testing eight datasets at once, and report the across-dataset test separately.} Eight independent tests at $\alpha$ = 0.05 produce at least one false positive 34\% of the time (\S3.4).
\item \textbf{Sweep the constants you chose without thinking.} Our own mechanism claim reaches significance at one bilinear rank and at none of the other three, though the ranks are mutually indistinguishable (\S5.6). We would not have known without the sweep.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{For anyone deploying with uncertainty estimates.}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Check mean prediction-set size before you check anything else.} It separated the three models whose minority coverage collapses from the twelve whose does not, with no overlap and no labels required (\S6.2). It is the cheapest deployment check in this paper.
\item \textbf{Use class-conditional conformal on imbalanced endpoints.} Marginal conformal met its 90\% target while covering 9.7--14.1\% of actives; the class-conditional variant restored 87--91\% at a visible and reportable cost in set size (\S6.2).
\item \textbf{Do not temperature-scale before conformalizing a binary task.} It cannot change the prediction set --- we prove it (\S6.3) --- and the empirical check agrees to the last molecule.
\item \textbf{Do not reach for APS or RAPS at two classes.} Both degenerate there (\S6.4). For regression intervals that vary informatively per molecule, use conformalized quantile regression (\S6.5).
\end{enumerate}


\section{Dataset quality: duplicate molecules with conflicting labels}

Canonicalising the SMILES in each benchmark reveals duplicates that raw strings hide, and in three of the eight the duplicates disagree with themselves. \code{python -m scripts.audit\_duplicates} reproduces the table.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lllll}
\toprule
dataset & rows & unique molecules & duplicate groups & groups whose labels conflict \\
\midrule
BBBP & 2,039 & 1,975 & 60 & 10 \\
ClinTox & 1,480 & 1,461 & 19 & 19 \\
ESOL & 1,128 & 1,117 & 11 & 6 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The other five datasets have no duplicates at all. Aspirin is one of the BBBP cases, present twice and labelled both permeable and not.

\textbf{This is not leakage, and the audit is what establishes that.} No duplicate group spans more than one split in any of the eight datasets, because identical molecules share a Bemis-Murcko scaffold and a scaffold split necessarily keeps them together. A random split would not have. That is a concrete, checkable argument for the scaffold protocol rather than an asserted one, and it is the second time in this paper that a property we adopted for one reason turned out to be load-bearing for another.

\textbf{It does bound achievable accuracy.} No model can be right about both copies of a molecule the benchmark labels two ways, so a component of every reported ClinTox error --- 19 self-contradictory groups in 1,480 molecules --- belongs to the data rather than to the architecture. We are not aware of this being accounted for in the numbers this benchmark is usually compared against, and we report it so that future work can subtract it rather than chase it.


\section{Limitations}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{No hyper-parameter tuning.} Every model uses one fixed setting held identical across architectures. This is what makes the comparisons fair and it leaves every absolute number untuned; a tuned version of any row here would be higher. We consider tuning one arm of a comparison against fixed-setting baselines to be the principal way a fusion result is manufactured, and we did not do it.
\item \textbf{Eight datasets, five seeds.} The across-dataset sign test cannot go below p = 0.0078, so a 7--1 split cannot reach significance on that statistic however large the effect.
\item \textbf{The comparison against the earlier pipeline runs on five datasets, not eight} (\S5.3), because that is where the pipeline's models exist. At n = 5 the sign test floors at p = 0.0625, so \emph{no} comparison in that table can reach p < 0.05 on that statistic, however large the effect. The per-dataset Holm column carries the weight there, and the conclusion we draw from it --- that the architecture clears the pipeline's base models but not its stacking meta-learner --- is correspondingly weaker evidence than the eight-dataset results.
\item \textbf{Our own headline mechanism result is not stable to a hyper-parameter} (\S5.6). The bilinear term separates from concatenation at every rank we tried, but only at r = 64 does it reach across-dataset significance, and the ranks are mutually indistinguishable. The effect is real; the p-value attached to it in this paper is partly an artefact of a constant chosen once. We found this because we swept it, and we report it rather than quoting the sweep only where it agrees.
\item \textbf{Two comparisons are cross-hardware} (\S7): the LoRA views against the CPU-trained graph reference, and the end-to-end ladder against the cached ladder. Both are unbiased in the five-split mean, so neither conclusion changes, but the within-device comparisons --- LoRA against its matched frozen control, and the cached ladder internally --- are the ones we lead with.
\item \textbf{Cliff sets are small} (10--34 molecules), and the fingerprint-similarity definition over-counts relative to a proper matched-molecular-pair analysis.
\item \textbf{Conformal calibration uses the validation split} for the models without out-of-fold predictions, which is also the early-stopping split; this biases the fitted map, not the test evaluation.
\item \textbf{Single architecture family.} We tested the mechanisms two specific proposals advocate, not those proposals' full published systems.
\end{itemize}


\section{Reproducibility and status}

Every number is generated from archived per-split predictions and metrics by scripts in the repository; the tables in this draft are built by \code{python -m scripts.make\_tables} and are not transcribed. The fixed hyper-parameter setting is machine-checked against the training code.

\textbf{Pending compute:} none. Every experiment this paper reports is complete. Two ablations named in the plan were deliberately not run and are not reported: two of the three leave-one-view-out arms (the third, and the only one a claim rests on, is in \S5.4), and a motif view that was never built. An Optuna study is implemented in the repository and has never been run; \S10 says why.


\section{Conclusion}

We built the measurement before the model, and the measurement is what paid.

\textbf{What it returned is usable today.} The expensive fusion block can be replaced by a gate 71$\times$ smaller with no measurable loss, and the graph view can be removed outright for a 13$\times$ training speed-up and one fewer library to install --- findings worth more to a practitioner than the architecture they came from. Mean prediction-set size separates the models whose minority coverage collapses from those whose does not, with no overlap and without needing a single label, which makes it the cheapest pre-deployment check we know of for the failure mode that matters most in a screening context. Temperature scaling provably cannot alter a binary conformal set, so a step many pipelines perform can simply be dropped. And recording which accelerator produced a number, then averaging over five splits, removes an error that moved 18\% of single-split results by more than the effect sizes this field reports.

\textbf{What it withheld is the reason to believe the rest.} The mechanisms we implemented work as specified --- verified, not assumed --- and do not beat a descriptor MLP on these benchmarks. Two published external baselines do not beat a two-layer graph network. Gate weights reorganise when a 0.4\%-weight view is removed, so they should not be read as importance. Our own mechanism claim reaches across-dataset significance at one bilinear rank and at none of the other three, though the ranks cannot be told apart. A protocol that returns only confirmations is not measuring anything; this one returned the efficiency result and the diagnostics \emph{and} refused the headline we started out wanting, from the same eight datasets and the same six splits.

The transferable claim is not about any architecture. It is that an evaluation strong enough to be trusted when it disappoints you is also strong enough to find the savings a weaker one walks past --- and that on these benchmarks those savings are large, immediate, and were sitting underneath a result nobody had reason to question.
